utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, had you concluded your examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. There will be an additional, I think, 15 minutes which includes one document and five photos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, let's begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Konings.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If we could retrieve 65 ter number 0323, please, and I'm interested in the second and third page.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And while that's being retrieved, yes, we see it already. Lieutenant-Colonel, do you recognise this document, the cover page of it?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, I neglected to say that in the absence of Judge Mindua, Judge Harhoff and I sit pursuant to the provisions of Rule 15 bis.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, if we can go to the second page of this document, which is the third page altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Can we please move to the next page, the third page. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And do you see, Lieutenant-Colonel, at the top of the page under paragraph 3, a few lines about impact analysis?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If you can briefly familiarise yourself with this paragraph. Now, the paragraph talks about an investigation into -- into this shell, that the firing of that shell that you investigated, and it talks about this UNMO report, 170 degrees. Is that your report? Is that your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was our conclusion, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And it also talks about the French engineers' report. To what is that a reference to?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that is a reference to a group of French engineers that did an investigation on the same moment as we did the investigation, and I think it refers to the French soldiers we saw on the movie -- on the video movie, yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And do you know roughly how much 2.850 mills equals in normal degrees?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is roughly the same as 170.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And then the paragraph also talks about the other four impacts which had a -- 220 to 240 degree firing point. Was that the conclusion you arrived to as you testified yesterday?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. Can you restate that question once more.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. You told us yesterday that you investigated the other four rounds, and you came to a conclusion as to the direction of fire.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That the 220 to 240 degrees of the other four rounds is our conclusion from our investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, apparently these paragraphs now seeks to talk about the difference between the two directions, one being 170 degrees and the other being 220 to 240 degrees; and mind you, they talk about two different instances; the first shell and the other four shells. And it gives an explanation at the end. The last sentence says, "There are several reasons for this apparent anomaly," and it goes on to say, "The most probable explanation is that the tail or body of the mortar struck a building on its flight path, which caused a different crater displacement pattern." Do you find this explanation correct in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my opinion, that is a theoretical explanation, and I don't believe that this is possible in practice. Of course, it's possible in practice that the mortar shell struck the roof or a part of the roof and gets other trajectory; but, in my opinion, if it struck the roof, it's thrown out of its trajectory in a quite severe way, in such a way that it will land on the ground in -- and can end up as a -- as a non-exploded device. In other words, it's a possibility, but in my opinion it's a theoretical possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If you look at the crater that was behind you yesterday, the -- the impact on the ground, is that consistent with what you just heard; the projectile hitting the roof?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the crater we saw, and the crater was which was on the photograph yesterday, was a, let me put it this way, a regular, normal mortar crater; a crater caused by a mortar projectile as we had seen many more before in Sarajevo. And if the projectile has hit the roof, then it only can be very, very slight hit, which didn't cause any change or hardly any change in the trajectory. That's to put it in another way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Excuse me. Does this mean that if it hit something like, for instance, a roof, then what I understand you're saying is that then it is really impossible to determine with any accuracy where it came from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I'm saying is what I tried to explain is that when it hits the roof severely, it will -- then the last part of the trajectory, the last metres of the trajectory, will be a total -- different from before, which will throw the projectile to another direction, with the possibility that it will even not explode. That's the point. And having seen the crater, which was a normal crater, I doubt that the projectile hit the roof at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, would you be able to tell us what forces would be -- would have been occupying the area of 220/240 degrees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think I understand your question with the forces occupying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Assuming -- well, there is a reference there paragraph 3 to a discrepancy. On the one hand, we have the first reports recording the bearing to the firing point at 170 degrees. So that presumably would -- would give an indication of the direction from which the firing came. And so I would be interested to know, if you do know, if have you the information, as to what forces would have been present in that area if one pinpointed 170 degrees; similarly, I would be interested to know, if you have the information, what forces would have been present in the area in relation to a firing point of 220 to 240 degrees.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Today, I don't have the specific information anymore. I cannot recall about who was exactly in what area. What I can say is that no matter you take 170 degrees or you take 220, it's all a rough southern direction; 180 degrees is south. That equals with the south part of the city of Sarajevo. And since the whole city, the biggest part of the city was surrounded by Serb troops and also in the in the biggest part around Sarajevo Bosnian army troops were opposing Serb troops in trenches and in other military emplacements, there were numerous troops from both sides in the area between 170 degrees and 220 up to 240. And to say exactly who was where, I cannot tell you about that. We had some of the information during our stay in Sarajevo. We, of course, had contacts with the UNPROFOR HQ in Sarajevo. We knew who was where; but exact detailed information, I cannot give you anymore today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Because, as I recall, your evidence yesterday was that the -- it's difficult to determine the specific origin of the fire, and you had told us why. I think it had something to do with the lack of information about the charge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is absolutely correct. If you don't know the charge, you don't know the place of origin. If you know the charge and if you know the angle of impact -- the estimated angle ever impact, then you can trace back the point of origin. And in the case of the round of 170 degrees, we have connected that with the reports of our OP1; and in the case of the four rounds, I cannot recall without studying the documents whether we had another report on that, from other OP, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, your evidence is that whether you talk 170 degrees or 220, 240, the area covered by that range is the southern area of Sarajevo; and in that area, generally one would find troops of both sides.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as my information recalls today, in that complete area were -- were troops from both sides involved. There were confrontation lines running south of the city, as they were also north of the city. And without knowing the charge the five rounds were fired with , you cannot determine the point of origin. You need other proofs for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Lieutenant-Colonel. Just one last question. Is your testimony that you will find it unlikely that the first and the four other shells came from the same place? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I disagree with the report of G2 of UNPROFOR. To my opinion, the two -- the first round and the later four of the other four, it's a very good possibility that they came from -- from different points of origin. You can speculate a lot about that, but I still stick to what the investigation we did on the spot. That's the only thing I can reasonably say, because I was there. I saw what my people did. I saw what I saw, and I still stick to the conclusion that it's 170 degrees; and for that -- for that reason, I only can say that to my opinion the five rounds came from two different gun positions, which is not very specific, because in the months before we had rounds in the city, mortar rounds from every direction, from south, but also from north. So they came from every direction. So the pattern was for us evaluating what happened that day quite normal. So there was for us no discussion whatsoever that it could have been two different gun positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. If we could move to the next -- to page 6 of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If you look at the left side of your screen, Lieutenant-Colonel, do you see this document?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you tell us what it is?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's an a document from the -- the engineers cell from the Sector Sarajevo of UNPROFOR, and it gives the results, I think, from the engineer group which did an investigation on the same spot as we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And if we move to the next page, please, which is a chart. It will be helpful if we can turn the chart around. Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you recognise this chart, Lieutenant-Colonel?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise it. I have seen it before this day, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And can you explain to Your Honours the -- the line that goes from what's called "impact" towards the bottom, slightly to the right of the page.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's the established line of fire by the French engineers, which is 2.850 mills or that equals 170 degrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think it says, "160 degrees?"

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, 160. Yes, it says 1-6-0 degrees, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If, Mr. President, that could be exhibited.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P357, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, to conclude this, and just to make it clear, in the course of your investigation - and you have talked about that mainly yesterday and also briefly today - based on the various elements you had at your position, did you come to the conclusion as to who, which side of the conflict, fired the deadly shot that you investigated at Markale?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Taking all the facts together, and especially the fact that nobody on OP1, neither Knustad or Major Paul Conway, did see or hear that morning any outgoing round, 120-millimetre; even stronger, there was no fire whatsoever to what I could establish, we came to the conclusion that the killing round must have come from the other side of the mountains, from a distance at least above, let's say, one and a half or two kilometres, which is behind the mountain range in the south part of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And who, Lieutenant-Colonel, occupied those positions behind the mountain range in the south part of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge, at that period, it were the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Lieutenant-Colonel. Now, that day, on the 28th or on the 29th of August, did you investigate the killing of a girl? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And where did that incident occur?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It happened in central part of the old city in a living block, a flat apartment block, and three girls were playing on the inner yard. And one rocket was hit that inner yard, and one young girl of four years old was killed and two others were injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you remember the calibre of the weapon that killed that girl?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a 128-millimetre rocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And do you remember the source of fire?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In combination with, and observing, an observation from our own team base, the rocket was fired from behind the ridge we called Sharpstone, which is the north part of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And who occupied that positions behind the ridge, which you called Sharpstone?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That ridge was occupied by Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me come to last two short topics. The first one is sniping. You told us yesterday that there was sniping towards the team base in Sedrenik. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that I told you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, how often did sniping occur in that area, and I'm talking about sniping against UNPROFOR or, indeed, civilians.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give any numbers on that because, well, we didn't get all the information; and in other cases, it was nearly not to count, and it must have been numerous, numerous times, as well, again, civilians as against at least our -- our team. So I cannot give an answer. It happened especially in the period up to the beginning of July. It happened nearly every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what was the source of fire?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We -- we were not able in 100 per cent of the cases to establish that; but in a number of cases - and I cannot give you any percentage; I cannot recall anymore - the fires came from, again, from that ridge, Sharpstone.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And my last issue, Mr. President, Your Honours, is I would like to show you five photographs. Lieutenant-Colonel, did you give to the OTP recently, I think it's 30 photographs which you took during your duty in Sarajevo in 1995?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I gave the OTP some photographs, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: This is 65 ter number 03034, please, and if we could go to the second photo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Can you tell Their Honours what this photo depicts.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This photo depicts a -- the biggest part of the old city, the old part of the city of Sarajevo, and the picture is taken from OP1.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And can you identify a few features on this photograph, if you can?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: One feature was very easy to recognise. In the central, left part is the old, burned library, the famous library, which was a very known marking point for us as UNMOs being on OP1.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you see it on -- on your screen?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you please mark it.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And please attach letter A next to it.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And do you see other features in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is not so clear as I thought. But in this area, here, somewhere here in this area - I draw it a bit the rough because I cannot give the exact location - there was my team base located; the north part of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please attach a letter B next to it.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If we could move to the next photo, which is number 5 in this range. Yes. I think it need to be saved. Mr. President, I would like to tender all the 30 photographs, so Your Honours can look at them. But I will only discuss five of them, so I don't know whether we need to individually --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I'm beginning to get a little wary of the practice of admitting things without seeing them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If Your Honours want it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But how many do you really need?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: -- it's just an illustration of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, just do four or five. But Mr. Tapuskovic has a point.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I also noticed that, but I didn't have time to take a look at it either today or yesterday and I check with my colleague. I also received some other photographs, but they were taken away from me so I don't have a chance to complete my examination. Therefore, it is difficult to analyse these things if one doesn't receive the material in time, and I hardly ever manage to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, when did you receive them?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were 11 or 12 photographs. I looked at them yesterday. These were the photographs from Spicasta Stijena. But after 20 minutes, they were taken away from me; therefore, I didn't have an opportunity to look at them closely. I just glanced at them and then Mr. Waespi took them away from me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, what is going on?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, that calls for an explanation. The photos were disclosed on a CD on Saturday, and I just gave my colleague, yesterday, the originals which I had with me, just to -- as a complimentary from my side. But we needed them because, as you see, the picture themselves are not that clear on the screen. So in case the witness wouldn't be able to recognise it on the screen, I have the originals. I am happy to give the originals back to counsel but the photos have been disclosed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. So it seems as though the photos were disclosed to you on a CD, on Saturday, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Even if that is the case, I didn't have a chance at all to confer with the accused since Saturday. After having looked at these photograph, it is totally impossible for me to deal with this, because I have more important matters to deal with than the photographs. My duty is to focus on more important issues, and I didn't have enough time for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I only show five photographs. The photographs are from very easily distinguishable positions like OP1, like the team base in Sedrenik, like "Sniper Alley," features we're all very familiar and certainly the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll just show four or five, so we'll deal with it in that way, Mr. Tapuskovic. He will only show four or five.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we can move on to the next photo which is number 5, yes, please, the previous one which was the second of that range.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: To be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P358, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What does this photo depict, Lieutenant-Colonel?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This picture is, again, taken from the surrounds of OP1. It, again, pictures the city of Sarajevo, but with a look more to the west of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. Lieutenant-Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If that could be admitted, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P359, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The next exhibit is number 12 in this range, and I will give the originals again to the Defence of these five photos after my examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What is depicted here, Lieutenant-Colonel?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the actual OP1 in the time that we were trying to -- to build some protection for ourselves, and it, again, give as view on the even more western part of the city of Sarajevo. You can see just right of my head - I'm the person on the left - you can see the twin towers. And close to that in every circumstance, you can see the Holiday Inn hotel, which was quite a known feature in those days on every news screen in the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And can you please circle the twin towers. And while that is it being done, can you remind us, again, the location of your colleague Knustad, when he informed you about the -- what he heard or not heard on the 28th of August.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Twin towers are here, and Mr. Knustad -- Major Knustad and Major Conway were on this exact location, where I am standing now on this picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please attach letter A depicting the twin towers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If that could be an exhibit, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P360, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The next and second-to-last picture is number 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, I give you 15 minutes at the break to consult.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'll give you 15 minutes at the break to consult with the accused on these photographs, so that we'll take an extended break so that you have an additional 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Konings, do you recognize this photograph?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recognize that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What does it depict?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is taken from our team base in the Sedrenik area, and the hill you see on the back is the hill where the confrontation line was running. And when you follow the hill to the right, where the forest are starting, around the edge is the so-called Sharpstone area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Lieutenant-Colonel. And the last photo I would like to show to you --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, that needs to be tendered, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P361, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If we can go to number 21, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you tell us what that photo depicts?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a photo driving in east direction on "Sniper Alley" inside Sarajevo, and on the left-hand side, the building with the yellow-brown colour on it is the Holiday Inn hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can it be exhibited, please, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P362, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I don't have any further questions. And here are the originals of the photos for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tapuskovic to cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have or will have sufficient time today to examine Mr. Konings.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Konings. My name is Branislav Tapuskovic. I'm Defence counsel for General Dragomir Milosevic. I would like to ask you a few questions with a view to clarifying certain matters that were discussed yesterday and today. In order to save time as much as possible, can we shed some light on a few issues. First of all, we have just seen these photographs. We saw the place where you and your observation team were. Can you tell me: From that position to this location, how long or how big a distance was it to the separation line?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the OP1 I think it roughly was about 1.000 metres, maybe less, and from the team base, about the same distances.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, it is fair to say that both armies were up in the hills.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The confrontation line was running on a changing matter with a lot of curves through all the hills and mountains. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were you ever in a position to measure the distance between the BH army forces and the forces of the army of Republika Srpska expressed in metres or whatever? Can you be specific on that?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can be very specific. We had no means and no possibilities whatsoever to measure the distance between the two forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: According to information that I have on file, I would like to ask you the following: Are you aware that on several occasions UNPROFOR had submitted a request to the BH army for your observation post to be located on the separation line, and that the BH army did not allow that to happen?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of these UNPROFOR requests to -- to the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The OP1 had a direct view of Colina Kapa, which is situated on Trebevic on the opposite side. There was another observation post there, an UNPROFOR observation post. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not -- you should have to show me that on a map. I'm not familiar anymore -- enough anymore with the names of Colina Kapa and Trebevic to say exact -- to give you an exact answer. So if you could -- if we could have a map with the positions on it, I can say. But I'm not familiar anymore with the names of Colina Kapa and Trebevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any idea at all, if you don't know where Colina Kapa was, then you were not able to tell me who occupied the positions there, whether the BH army or the VRS. It's a hill that is 940 metres high.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I told already that I cannot recall today the detailed information about the positions of the BH army and the VRS as we had it then, during that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So you are claiming that all the hills surrounding Sarajevo were held by the VRS.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not what I'm saying, and I didn't say that at all. I was saying that the hills and the mountains around Sarajevo were occupied by both parties - I can recall that I said that before - and that the confrontation line was running on the hills and mountains around Sarajevo. That's what I was saying. And I have no -- today I have no exact detailed memory anymore about who was exactly where because the positions changed every day. That's what we knew. And again, I don't have the exact date anymore available today.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, is it correct that the confrontation line that you mentioned, in case of Sedrenik, ran elsewhere at the foot of the hills around Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were certain parts that the confrontation line came to the foot of the hills. In Sedrenik, it runs across the hills, and we were especially focussing on the ridge Sharpstone, which we knew was in the hands of the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: However, the distance between the positions of the two armies was not a big one at this particular location; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fact that there was a confrontation line means that the two armies were quite close together. But as I told you, I have no information and we had no information during that period on exactly how far they were from each other. So I cannot -- I cannot and I will not speculate on any distance today.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: On this topic, Mr. Konings, let me ask you this: Concerning the hills to the north, such as Zuc and Hum, which were easily visible because one of them had a TV tower on that, did those hills overlook Sarajevo and had a commanding view from that side?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall the hill with the TV tower on it. That was outside my area of responsibility, but it had a commanding view, as far as I know, on Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You know that this is where the BH army positions were. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I can recall, there were BH army positions; and somewhere below the TV tower, there was also an UNMO team.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Lieutenant-Colonel, can we go back for a moment to the two documents shown to you a while ago by Mr. Waespi. The Baxter report dated the 8th of September; is that correct? That was as many as ten days after the Markale incident. If is it dated 8th of September, that means it was compiled ten days after the incident. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are pointing to the G2 UNPROFOR report, because I don't have the report here in front of me, so if it has been dated the 8th of September, but I have not seen that report either in Sarajevo. I have seen that report only the first time when I came here in the office of Mr. Waespi. So, if it says 8 September, it says 8 September. That is very simple. I cannot give you any extra information on that date whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This will suffice, Lieutenant-Colonel. Equally, we can say that about the document prepared by engineers and dated the 6th of September. So you're saying, again, that you first saw it the other day when you were examining it with Mr. Waespi?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I have not seen these reports in my period in Sarajevo, but that was quite normal - I have to add that to my declaration - since UNMOs were supposed to work impartially. So we never received that report on our level, maybe on the higher UNMO level in Zagreb or in Sarajevo. But on the teams, we were only confronted with our own reports and the summarized reports which our senior military observer made every day which he sent to Zagreb. That is the only reports that we were seeing, so it was quite normal that I didn't have a view on every other report which was written by either UNPROFOR or by the French sector commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Konings, I will now deal with a few documents that you worked on and that were prepared on the 28th of August, 1995 and another one compiled on the 29th of August, 1995, as well as a report compiled by Lieutenant-Colonel Janvier addressed to the UN Secretary-General Mr. Kofi Annan. Can we please look together at document 65 ter number 198, P85. Yesterday, you analysed this document with the Prosecutor, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have this document displayed on our monitors.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I have this report in B/C/S; but in order not to spend too much time on it, let's first look at the date. It says, "the 28th of August." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: "Patrol leader, Colonel Konings;" is that right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: There's the general part of this report and your tasks. And under item 2, where you mention the bearings or the azimuth, I will read to check whether you abide by that. "The bearings in combination with the estimate angle of impact could not provide evidence of the origin of fire since it is not known with which charge the projectile had been fired." Do you abide by what you said on that day up to this date?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to ask the interpreters to use another word for "abide," because I cannot place that correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you "stand by." That's what it means.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand. I still abide or I still stand by what I said or what I wrote in that part of my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to read the whole document. On that date, you were in touch with an investigation team of the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So if we look at the very end of your report, i.e., item 3, that's the last paragraph of your report dated 28th of August, 1995, and it read as follows --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: This is not item 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Please identify the correct item. Mr. Waespi to the rescue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: It's on the last page -- the second page. It is called, "5 Patrol leader's remarks," and it's subsection 3 of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. I omitted to mention that we should have moved to another page. Page 2, last paragraph on this page, which reads, item number 3 -- These are patrol leader's remarks, and this is you, Mr. Konings. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's still correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It reads as follows: "The investigation team tried very hard to prove that the attack came from the Bosnian Serb side." Is this -- does this mean that it was the Muslim investigators who tried very hard to convince you that the shot came from the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the investigation team meant in point 3 of this point -- I mean, the team from the Ministry of the Interior, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And to round this up, it goes on to say: "Due to the normal use of heavy mortars," and this is now your view; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which point are you aiming at now? Oh, the next sentence. I see. Yes. That is my view, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then you concluded: "But there is no hard proof on this fact." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is -- that is correct on the time that I stated that there was no hard proof, since we didn't know the charge that was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did your views coincide with the position of Lieutenant-Colonel Janvier, conveyed to Mr. Annan, Secretary-General of the UN, which says -- it's document DDD-10 [as interpreted], also dated the 28th of August, so the same date when you prepared your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have that document called up so that Mr. Konings can have a look at it. That's page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This is being sent by General Janvier addressed to Mr. Annan. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking this to me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. He is asking to you confirm.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think so. I have also not seen this report when I was in Sarajevo, so I'm not a person whether you should ask the question whether this report was sent by General Janvier to Mr. Kofi Annan. I cannot give you any -- if the report is here, I think it has been sent. But I'm not the guy to tell you exactly what has happened with this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's see to what extent you can help.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we look at page 3 of the English version of this document, and I have a question for Mr. Konings in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It talks about UNPROFOR, Sector Sarajevo, the date is the 28th of August, 1995. If you need time, please go ahead and read the whole paragraph; however, further down, there's a sentence that speaks about mortar shells and it says that it is very difficult to -- it is impossible to determine the level of charge used to fire the projectiles. Can you see that sentence, sir? And is this your position as well that you expressed in your reports, dated also the 28th of August? That was my question.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm still reading the paragraph, so if you grant me some extra minute, I will be grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This point of view on the fact that you have to know the charge of the mortar to establish a fixed position where the mortar was fired is at the same -- the same point of view as we wrote in our patrol report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now show Mr. Konings document 65 ter 02605, dated --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the counsel please repeat the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, can you repeat the date?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 29th of August, which means the day after the report we've just seen, which was dated the 28th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you see it, sir? So you have this report in front of you. It's another report compiled by your patrol, only now it's dated the 28th of August, and again Lieutenant-Colonel Konings is cited here as the patrol leader. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It has its general part which reads that the task was assigned by the UNMO headquarters in Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, since every task we did was -- was given us by the UNMO HQ.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The next sentence reads: "This report is related to the UNMO patrol report issued on the 28th of August, 1995." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Then you mentioned some meetings. But under item 4, there are two paragraphs. Item 4 talks about meetings and the goals of the meetings, and you also mention some aspect from the previous report. And under lower case A, you say, "In the time when the five impacts happened, UNMOs working at OPS --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: The English version is completely illegible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, the English version is illegible, so read slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's page 2, I forgot to mention that. I will read it slowly. "At the time when five impacts happened, UNMOs and ICZ," abbreviation unknown, "team working at OP, neither," then this section is illegible, "neither from Bosnian army territory," illegible, "Bistrik and Colina Kapa." It means at that stage you knew where Colina Kapa was. So when you wrote this report, you knew very well where Bistrik and Colina Kapa were; is that true?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I stated it there, then I knew and I have not said that I didn't know it at the time. I cannot recall the exact location today, 12 years after the date. So the specific details of the complete area around Sarajevo, to mention the names, I can only designate if you need me to do that on a map, not from recollection. Everything that I wrote here in this report, with names and suffice to say it was done on that day and was correct on that day, and I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This paragraph ends with your stating that you were unable to establish that this projectile had been fired from the Bosnian Serb positions either. That's how this paragraph ends, with this statement of yours.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the paragraph is very hard to read on the screen, so if we -- if somebody could enlarge it a bit, because some of the words I cannot see.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This document has been disclosed to me by the Prosecution, and it says: "Neither from the territory of the BH army, nor from the territory of the Bosnian Serb army." Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What paragraph is that, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2 lower case A.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It says that the UNMOs on OP1 did not hear outgoing rounds either from the territory of the Bosnian Serb army terrain or from the Bosnian Serb army terrain. It doesn't say anything further. It just said they didn't any outgoing round from their vicinity from Bosnian army territory either from Serb army territory, and that's just stating the simple fact that they didn't hear anything on outgoing rounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] .

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But it also says that they didn't see either. Were you referring to radar operation at that time?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not referring to -- to a radar operation because we had no radars. The radar which available inside Sarajevo was acting under the command of UNPROFOR and completely independent from our operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: We'll go back to this, but let's finish this document first. In the remarks made by the patrol leader, item 3, last sentence, reads: "That all the reports as stated in the first report remain unchanged and valid." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not -- I'm not able to see this sentence on the screen. So before I will say anything about that, I need to see that sentence on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That's a technical matter. I have this here, underneath it's your signature, Lieutenant-Colonel Konings. Patrol leader?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I fully believe what you are saying, but I don't see that specific sentence and I don't see my signature. Now I think I see something. Yeah, I wrote that during that day, and I signed it as well. Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So, you stand by your findings in all points, and this report that augments your findings that nothing was heard convinced you further that your first report was accurate. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The second report supports the first report, and the second report includes also the opinion of the two UNMOs on OP1, that they neither heard or saw outgoing rounds, and that were the pure facts what we as an UNMO team could gather on that two days; nothing more and nothing less.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, first of all, I would like to have document 65 ter 02065, and I would like that document to be marked as a Defence exhibit. The document has not been tendered by the Prosecution, and I would like to have this document entered as a Defence exhibit. It's the document dated the 29th of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D118, Your Honours -- Sorry. Registry's correction: D117.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Konings, not to loose any time now, I would like to read once again the basic position from the document of the 28th, which states: "The azimuth combined with the impact angles do not prove the origin of the fire, because --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters are not reading from the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, not that. I apologise. The last sentence, where you said that you set off from the fact that probably because of the usual use of heavy mortars, it probably came from the Serb side. Is that what you said a little bit earlier? The investigation team put in a lot of effort to indicate or to show that the attack came from the Serbian side, which probably, due to the usual use of heavy mortars. Is that what you said earlier?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, it's not clear to me what you are putting to the witness. Are you putting something that is in the report?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. It's the first report. I asked the witness about this earlier, and he said that that was his position, that it was probably fired from the Serb side since there was use of heavy mortars. But there was no firm proof of that. That is the document of the 28th.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is that how it was, Mr. Konings? Because we don't want to waist any more time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me hear Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just to be helpful, it's the earlier document, P85, and again second page, the third point on the second page, just before the body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Yes, Lieutenant-Colonel, what is your response to that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My response is the following: On one hand, there was on that day, and also the day after, new hard proof that the round came from came from Serb-held territory, just because of the fact that we didn't know with which charge the round was fired. I'm talking about the kill round, the one which landed in Markale. That's the first point. The second point I want to make is that after talking to my UNMOs, who were working on OP1, and hearing their statements, which are in the second report, they didn't hear or see any outgoing round from neither Serb territory or Bosnian army territory. And the third part of my statement is being there already for nearly five months in Sarajevo, and having seen the way that 120-millimetre mortars were used, I came to the conclusion that to the analysis that there was nothing different from what we had witnessed already months before, in all the months before, which was purely, very simple, the use of a single mortar rounds shot anywhere in the city; not aimed against military target, but in a way that I called in another report as a harassing fire against civilian people. But, again, I stated that in both reports there was no hard proof, no hard evidence whatsoever. The fact that I stated that this, to my opinion, came from the Serb side was an analysis to my report which went up to in the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Your assertion was that the these had to have been mortars because you had never heard 120-millimetre mortars being fired from the territory of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that the gist of you're assertion?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are of course many, many things to say about this question. There are many factors to influence everything what happens; and the fact that we never or hardly ever saw Bosnian army troops using 120-millimetre mortars inside the territory of the city of Sarajevo, so of the inside of the confrontation line, I never have seen it or heard myself personally, neither did my personnel see it. There is, in one occasion, a report that was not of my own team but from another team that a Bosnian army team fired a mortar from inside the city to the outside of the city. So we had never any proof, visual proof from my team, either OP1, either during patrols, either from the team base that the Bosnian army used 120s from the inside of the city to fire at Serb positions outside the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like your permission regarding this problem that we are facing right now, and that is with the aid of the interpreters - we're not going to need more than a minute or two - I would like to present a document which shows that only -- or just on the 4th of July, 1995, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina fired 120-millimetre shells, and this is according to the report by the BiH army, the commander of the 12th Division. I have a lot of these documents, but it indicates that a month and a half before the 28th in one day, or over several days, one hundred 120-millimetre mortar shells were fired. This is a document of the 4th of July, 1995, signed by the brigade commander; the commander of the 12th Division, Fikret Prevljak, in active combat, considerable quantities of MTS were spent; and then it is said 60 -- that 80 to 200 mines [as interpreted]; and 120-millimetre, one hundred items. So according to this one document, alone, on the 7th --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Instead of a speech, just put a question. What is the question? You want to show that document? Is it to go on the ELMO? Is it an e-court document?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it's a document of the B and H army, an order that was issued by the commander of the forces in Sarajevo, Fikret Prevljak. It is not translated. And in view of what I heard yesterday from Mr. Konings, I would like to place this document -- to be given an ID number, because I see, judging by this document, that on the 7th of July, according to the document of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina - and it's a document that I received from the archives of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina - in one day 100 such mortar shells were fired. It can be marked for identification. I'm just showing Mr. Konings the following.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear on the 7th of July from Sarajevo --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Waespi is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not doubting that my friend, Mr. Tapuskovic is quoting correctly. But before a document is shown, and in fact read out to the witness, I would love to see the document, even if it's not translated, so I can see what is read from so there is a record of what is put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you have -- how many copies do you have?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since the break will be with us soon, I'm going to give it to Mr. Waespi to look at over the break, and then ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. We'll take the break now and the break is 20 minutes, and I will give you an additional 15 minutes. And I make it clear that that is to allow you to consult with your client, because you were not able to consult with him before on the -- the photographs. We are adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this document that we discussed before the break, can we please have it on the ELMO and then the interpreters can translate it. It's just a few sentences. I'm going to read very slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: "Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina the command of the 12th Division, STR/number 022-2-182, Sarajevo, the 4th of July, 1995." And relating to that, I would like to ask Mr. Konings if on the 4th of July and thereabouts he was in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to check my records, but I cannot say precisely whether I was specifically on that day in Sarajevo, because on two occasions I was on leave. So, I cannot say yes, or I cannot say no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In the statements of yours that I read, and that I'm going to deal with later, there are five of your statements. You did not once mention that you left Sarajevo between the 5th of May and October, when you actually left Sarajevo for good?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, that's correct, because that was never asked of me. And since I was questioned specifically about the Markale incident, 28th of August, and in that period I was present in the city, so have I been on leave during -- twice, a short period in my -- in my time in Sarajevo, that's correct. But I cannot recall the exact timings anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But I have this report, and I have 30 more such reports, but I picked this one and now I'm going to read. It's the combat report of the 1st Corps for that day, and under item 2: "Our forces," and then 2.4, it says: "Logistics."

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, I can do it in re-examination, although I still only have the B/C/S version. But in all fairness, maybe it should be into context, the first sentence starts that the Serbian army started to attack with artillery civilian objects, that's number one; and later in that paragraph, he talks about that UNPROFOR headquarters were engaged by the Bosnian Serb army. So I think it's fair to put it on to the record before going to the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic. It's a short document. Let's have everything in context.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, absolutely, all of this, yes. This is a document that will be used by the Prosecution and by the Defence. I'm asking this in the context of the claim by the witness that he had never heard a single mortar shell of 120-millimetres being fired from Sarajevo. This is a document that speaks of how on the 4th of July, 1995, 100 such shells were fired of 120-millimetres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Proceed. Mr. Waespi, you may re-examine on this, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Also, as a point of caution, nowhere it say this is document that these shells were fired from Sarajevo. I don't see that in this document. It talks about the 12th Division. It talks about some brigades, but I'm not familiar and I wonder whether the witness is familiar where these brigades and divisions were located.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may react, Your Honour. I can clarify this very simple. If can I recall, I have stated that I haven't seen or heard 120-millimetre mortars fired from my part of Sarajevo, from my area of operations, where my team was operating. That area of operations was very small. It was a very small part of the city of Sarajevo, which stretches in length of kilometres between the mountains. My area of responsibility was the central, old part of the city, excluding the confrontation lines. So when I say that I never heard or saw a 120-millimetre mortar being fired by the Bosnian army, it is from that specific area of responsibility; and, of course, in times during many days that there were heavy fightings in the confrontation line, we have witness that. We have filed reports on that. But the fire exchange during that days was so heavy that it was impossible for to us to say who was doing what, especially, and I have to stress that, with the very, very limited technical means UNMOs have available for doing their job. If you are from a distance, let's say one and a half kilometres or two kilometres, from an area where fighting is going on, and if you only have available a poor binocular and a very simple compass, then you are not capable, no matter how good your basic military skills are, to establish who is doing what. I cannot stress enough that I stay with what I stated before. I didn't see or didn't hear, neither did my team, 120 rounds coming out of my part of the city of Sarajevo. So it can be very well that the Bosnian army itself claimed that they fired 100 or maybe 200 rounds, but that has happened in another part of Sarajevo where none of my responsibility was and where I had no view of what was happening there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I take note of these remarks. This was signed by Commander Fikret Prevljak who was commanding units of the 12th Division that were entirely in Sarajevo. This was signed by the commander of the 12th Division who was acting from Sarajevo. So, please, I would like to read that he claims that in active combat, considerable quantities of MTS material and equipment was sent and spent and then he says: "100 pieces of 120-millimetre shells." So I would like to ask the witness how is it possible that you did not hear in one day so many shells of this type being fired.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, I can only stress what I said. We were not -- from my part of the city were no -- we didn't hear or see rounds be fired. Again, I didn't say we didn't hear the fighting around Sarajevo. Of course, you cannot overhear when there is a big fire exchange going on in the confrontation line or further away in the city. But we were ordered, specifically by our commanders, to watch our own area, to operate in our own area, and we were ordered not to speculate on anything else. So what we reported was that there was a big fire exchange going on in the confrontation line from grid X to grid Y during time A to time B. Not specifying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you, thank you. Mr. Tapuskovic, I think we have -- you have dealt with this now sufficiently. Please move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: My last question on this is: How did they then manage to identify on the 28th precisely by sound and other elements that 120-millimetre shell was fired on the 28th of August in 1995? How did they manage to determine that? Can they explain that when they did not identify any previously fired shells? How can they explain that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I--

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry. Let me give an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the facts you are now stating are not correct. We were previously able to identify 120 rounds, especially when it -- most of the times when we were able to identify it, it concerned single rounds. And a single round you can identify, especially when the area is more quiet. And now I'm coming to the point I want to make. On the 28th of August, there was no single shot fired during the whole day, only in the morning. Very early in the morning, at 8.00, there was a fire exchange from an another area in the say. It was quiet. It was a bright day, so sounds carry very far. Until the moment that this round was fired, the killing round, there was no fire exchange whatsoever. So there was -- we were not distracted by any other noise from fire exchanges from both sides. And that gives the explanation that in this case we could very clearly determine whether we heard something, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you said that we have exhausted the topic, I would just like to ask for this document to be a given an ID number as a Defence exhibit. I could keep asking more, but, of course, I'm going to abide by your instructions. But I would like to have there tendered and given an ID number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Chamber has heard enough. We have to make up our minds about the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. It's marked for identification pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be marked for identification as D118.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you for the time given to me to look at the photographs. After an analysis of the photographs, I would like to show the witness only one photograph; that's the 65 ter number 03034, page 21. No -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This photograph that we see in front of us, if I recall correctly, you said this is "Sniper Alley"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This building at the end, do you know that that used to be a government building -- the government building?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not -- I cannot recall that, what the original purpose of the building was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, understandable. But when we look at that building, does it not dominate -- isn't it a dominate feature in this street named "Sniper Alley"?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's a quite dominant feature.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you know that on the left-hand side, although you cannot see it in the photographs, there were even two higher buildings, the so-called Unis buildings. Do you remember that there were two higher buildings to the left of the ones that we see to the left in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall these buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure if the Prosecutor had tendered this for -- to evidence; and if not, I would like to tender it as a Defence exhibit, please. [In English] Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is in evidence as Prosecution Exhibit 362.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Konings, one more thing lest I should forget. A while ago you said that the 50 [as interpreted] shells had been fired from two different positions; four from one position and one from another position. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suspect that you mean that you point that the five shells. The translation says 50 shells, but I think you mean the five projectiles that were fired on the 28th of August, that day. My opinion was they were fired from two locations. If that is the idea, then my opinion on that day was that they were fired from two positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The one that hit Markale 2 was enough to hit the target; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know, first of all, what the exact target was because I was not at the -- at the firing location from the mortar. So it hit a target, but I don't know what the target was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe it wasn't clear enough. It was sufficient for one mortar to be fired for it to land at this specific location; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say that. I only can state the fact that one mortar round landed in the street, at Markale, and four other rounds landed someone hundred metres from there. So I cannot state anything more than -- than what I have seen there. I cannot speculate about the -- the orders the mortars -- the one mortars or the two mortars had to fire at. I don't know anything about the grids. They were ordered or the way they were fired. So I stick to the point that there was one mortar round falling into the street doing the killing work, and there were four others falling in another place a few hundred metres from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, when you spoke about the number of projectiles that have to be fired in order to engage a target and achieve something, on page 64, you said that at least two or more shots were required for at least one shell to hit a specific target. That's what -- what you explained yesterday on the page in the transcript that I quoted.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it's in the transcript, I possibly have said it or I'm sure I staid. But I think I referred -- yesterday, we were referring to the regular military use of 120-millimetre mortars. But before I go into anything further, I would like to read what I said yesterday before -- because otherwise I start -- we start discussing about something what I first would like to know myself again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm reading from the paper that I have in front of me. "In most cases, a specific procedure is being followed and" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Which page, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 60, line 4 of the working order --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Draft transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Of yesterday's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I apologise. I have pages starting 3.505 and going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is what has been provided by my colleague. All I can say is that it's page 60, line 4 of the draft version; otherwise, I don't know how I can help the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I have on my screen page 3.560, starting with the

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: certain source," and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm not going to waste any more time. I have exhausted this subject, and I will not go back to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask the witness in order for a certain result to be achieved by firing from mortars, 120 millimetres-- 122 millimetres, how many shots need to be fired in order to hit a desired target?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That depends on a lot of factors which will take at least an hour to explain the ballistics background. Let's put it this way, one round can hit a target. When you have sufficient data from the target you want to hit and from -- to influence your ballistic data like weather reports, like winter reports, et cetera, you are able to fire a round more or less in the area you want to have it. And if you have a grid from the target, you can use one round to try to hit it. You can be lucky; you can be unlucky. So to my opinion, the killing round, because that's where we are all talking about - let's not full around - the killing round can have been a lucky shot. But that, again, that fit into the pattern we saw for the months before; just firing single rounds into the city knowing that you were hitting always something. Well, and in this case, people were -- well, the round hit the street where a lot of people were around. And in other case it is hit the roof and did only some superficial damage. That's my opinion on that. So a single round when it hits the target, then it can do a lot of damage in this case; and for the same reason, it is would have -- that specific round would have landed 50 metre further away and hit the roof of a building.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You claim, therefore, that this was a randomly fired round that hit this specific location completely accidently?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You take my words wrong. All the fire which was done, to my opinion, was done randomly but with a certain pattern, and everybody knew that certain parts in the city - and I'm quite sure that the Serb army knew that as well - certain parts of the city were more interesting than the others. I yesterday referred to cross roads, to water collection points, so the use of the street where the Markale incident took place, which was a main, a main street, must have been known by both parties involved in the conflict then, in that period. So that information belongs to the intelligence gathering of any army in the world. So if you know that something is going on there or that a lot of people are gathered there, which was a normal pattern also in the days and months before, you can try to hit that area with one or more rounds, which happened that morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: We'll get back to that later. Now I'm going to follow my sequence of questions. First of all, is it fair to say that you have absolutely no medical knowledge, that you know nothing at all about any issues relating to medicine?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have some basic military medical knowledge. We have some medical training, but I'm definitely not a medicitian [sic] or a medical soldier, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, you said that after some 50 minutes you arrived at the scene, that you spent sometime there, and after that you went to the morgue. Would it be fair to say that that was about after an hour or one hour and a half?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You examined 40 people in the morgue. Can you tell me how long did the examination of these bodies take, and there were approximately 40 bodies?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure how long exactly, but it took a period of, let's say, about 15 minutes. We didn't examine the bodies one by one. What we always did was a general idea, a general view of what we saw to -- to bring that into our report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You know nothing about how long it takes for a person to lose all the blood from his or her body, a person who eventually died?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can give you no figures about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Also you know nothing about how the time of death is established. At that time, you knew nothing about that?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As I stated, I have been trained in basic military medical skills.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You never received a report on -- which would show the time of death of the persons who were already dead at that time?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never seen -- I have never received a report with times of deaths of people involved in that -- in that explosion, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In any case, after what we heard from you yesterday, would it be fair to say that not even then did you see dead bodies, nor did you do that ever when you visited the scenes and conducted on-site investigations?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not think I understand the question well, so could you rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 28th of August, 1995, I understand that the wounded had to be evacuated very speedily. But would it be fair to say that you didn't see any of those dead bodies, the 40 dead bodies, at the scene, except for body parts?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. That is what we stated yesterday, so that's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, you said that the effect that you observed was much more powerful than any among you including yourself had ever seen before. Is that what you said yesterday?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure that I used the word "powerful," but the scene I saw on that date was the most, how shall I put it? I cannot find the right English word for that. It was the most impressive scene that I saw in my period in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if I got the right translation. Instead of saying the "most impressive," I suppose you meant the most horrendous. The translation that I received said "most impressive." I would describe it as a terrifying sight.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Again, it's a bit tricky for me to -- to refer to what was said yesterday, because I don't have that text before me. The scene was horrendous, was terrifying, and, as I also told, was very tense. And that made it the most specific situation that I encountered and also my colleagues encountered so far in my period in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Given that so many casualties were there, around 120 of them, were you surprised that a 120-millimetre mortar shell could produce an overwhelming effect.
