Nowadays, we're seeing that this number of people are being killed in Iraq by 120 kilograms of explosives. Were you surprised to see 120 casualties as a result of a single round, mortar shell round?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived at the scene, at the first moment, of course, you are surprised by the sheer number of people involved in that. But when you are starting to work in the collection of the data and you see the area it happened, the environment, because that is of very big importance, you realise that one single projectile from that calibre can do the work. That is a combination of factors, as it is always in the -- in the use of artillery -- of mortar ammunition. The projectile exploded in the street between high buildings. That's the first factor, which means that the pressure of the projectile cannot get away. It's comprised in a smaller area. There were a lot of glass still in the buildings, so a lot of the buildings still had windows, and glass which is destroyed can do a lot of nasty things. And also the shrapnels of the projectiles, which are many thousands, could affect the people, and one extra factor is that it was very busy on the street. There were lots and lots of people on the street that morning. So when you count these factors together, then I think it's -- and looking to the power, the explosive power of 120 shell, which in our case in the Netherlands army, at least has five or I think even seven kilogrammes of TNT, concealed in a -- in a small area with high buildings around it, it's my conclusion that one projectile of that calibre can do the work.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, you said that you were surprised both by the political and military effects of this incident. Can you elaborate on that?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly could, but I don't see whether that is important for the further explanation of this point, so I -- I rather prefer not to answer this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, it's not for you to determine. I will determine that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, what do you mean "by the political and military effects of the incident," and explain how they are relevant to the issues?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since the witness himself said that he is unable to give me an answer to this, what I meant was this: Was he surprised in view of the fact what he found at the scene, that it was impossible to determine --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, are you --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you established that it was impossible to determine the origin of fire on the 28th of August. Does that correspond to your reports that we have been dealing with here?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't follow your question. I have stated many more times, many times during my explanation, yesterday and today, that we were not able to determine the origin of fire. You have seen that in the reports coming back, so that is what I can state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You determined the direction from which the fire came.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We determined, that's correct, the direction from the fire came.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The azimuth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But that is something different than the origin of fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic, move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But were you surprised that on that same evening all the world media said that this was done by the Serbian side? Were you surprised by that, in view of the fact that it was impossible to determine the origin, both by you and by General Janvier? Were you surprised to hear that?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can be very short in my answer. I was not surprised at all that evening, because I did not know anything about the international news and the international view. I was busy that evening dealing with this investigation team of the Bosnian Ministry of the Interior. I was busy commanding my team. And the most simple reason is that I did not know. So I could not be surprised by the international reaction, because we had no radio or television communication in our house since we had no electricity. I was completely shut off from information from the outside world, so I could not be surprised, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Konings, during your investigation of all of this to date, you have provided five statements on this topic to the Prosecutors and investigators. Do you recall providing five statements to the investigators and several directly to the Prosecutors. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It were numerous. So if you say it are seven, then probably it will be seven.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I said five; I don't know how it was translated.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. You said five, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall, and that way I don't have to look for that in the transcript, you said yesterday that there were rumours in Sarajevo that sometimes bodies were planted in places where they actually did not perish. Do you remember saying that yesterday, that there were such rumours?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that I said that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: These were rumours that you heard in Sarajevo itself; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown his statement that you gave on the 31st of May, 2006. That is document DD00-0621. Can we look at the first page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that that is the statement that you gave? I must go to this statement first. Is that your statement? Please look at the signature. Is that the statement of the 31st of May, 2006?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is my statement, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at paragraph 7 on page 3, the end of the paragraph; thus, paragraph 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Look at the end you said there, the last two sentences: "I never saw any evidence that bodies had been planted." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I stated that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then the next sentence: "I had been briefed upon arrival with UNPROFOR to be alert to the possibility of bodies being planted at scenes." Is that correct, that you were warned about this?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I stated that, so that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So these were not rumours, but UNPROFOR, of which you were a member, warned you that this was possible. So can we say, then, that these were not rumours?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's up to you to conclude that. To my opinion, even if UNPROFOR warned us of that, you can still call it rumours. So no matter what word you give it, we were warned for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And General Nicolai, was he your superior since he was the Chief of Staff of General Smith? You know who General Nicolai is?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know General Nicolai, but he was not my superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: On page 1039, lines 7 to 10, I asked General Nicolai the following: "Does this fit into what Van Baal told you that when talking about the highest state interest, ones own people could be sacrificed?" And Nicolai said that he did not rule out that possibility, that he does not rule that possibility that bodies could have been planted and that this could have been done for military and political interests of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and this is what General Nicolai stated here. Did you hear anything like that from the supreme commanders?"

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not hear anything in this way, as you state -- or as General Nicolai has formulated there, from my direct commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Even General Smith on page 3.414, lines 15 to 23, the UNPROFOR supreme commander for that region, stated that this was possible. This didn't reach you either, did it?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The orders from -- or the specific orders from either General Smith or General Nicolai were not given to us straight away. It has to be clear that UNMOs were in a separate chain of command. So the only people we were dealing with, especially on the level of the team leader, as I was, was my senior military observer. We had no contacts, and I repeat, no contacts with the UNPROFOR organisation, which we were basically no part of. UNMOs were not integrated in UNPROFOR in the chain of command. They had their own organisation with the chief military observer in Zagreb. Our reports and our orders went to Zagreb and came from Zagreb through the chain of command of the UNMOs. So anything General Smith or General Nicolai has stated or said in that period, I have never seen that or have seen it in a written --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I'm grateful for the Defence to point out the exact location of what General Smith said, and just to quote him correctly he said, and I quote him, "In theoretical fashion, it was possible." That is what General Smith said, which is slightly different to how he was quoted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We take note of that, yes. Mr. Tapuskovic, the Prosecutor spent two hours and 9 minutes; and at the end of this session, which is at 5.35, you would have had about two hours and 15 minutes. It's not my intention to allow you to go beyond that time, and you're not obliged to use all of that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I was just dealing with documents. I have five statements of this witness. If I do not put the most important things from these witness statements to the witness, I will absolutely not be in a position to point out all that you need to consider. The Prosecutor had the time that he was allowed and he was also granted an extension, so I most sincerely would like to request that you allow me a little by the more time so that I can put to the witness things from the statements. I think that it would be not be all right. I don't want to use the word "just," for me not to be allowed to complete my cross-examination. I kindly ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Proceed, and we will see how --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Proceed, and we will see how you get on at 5.35.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Regarding this question, I don't want to be going back to that, and any way these are the pages that I cited, so you will be able to refer to them. But your superior was a Danish man, Thomas Hansen, when he arrived. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall he was not Thomas Hansen but Torben Hansen, but the last name is Hansen and he was Danish, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: These are two different Hansens, is that what you're claiming?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not claiming anything. I just state when arrived in Sarajevo, the team leader of the team I was posted was a Danish captain; and to my recollection, his name was Torben Hansen and not Thomas Hansen, but the last name was definitely Hansen. I even have a picture of him so I know what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Well, let's, then, take it -- well, I don't know which Hansen to talk about now. Did you hear about Hansen' report, a Danish person -- now I'm not sure if that is a person who -- did you hear about that report, that according to their findings according to what the UNMO observers -- did you hear about that, that the television building a month before the 28th June, so that was two months before, was hit by an aerial bomb by representatives of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Everybody is fully familiar with this document, but the objection is it is not correct to say that it was hit by representatives of the ABiH. The document says that Mr. Hansen heard from somebody else that that person saw something happening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Hansen received a report from an UNMO officer to that effect -- an UNMO observer. You heard about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can clarify that quite easily. Since the date of the 28th of June now is appearing, I didn't hear that before. There was no way that we can talk about my Captain Torben Hansen, because he had left the mission already. And I don't know anything about this report whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, the plot thickens. So your Captain Hansen, you say Torben Hansen, he had left by the 28th.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I came in at the 4th of May; and as I recall roughly after a week or six, I took over the team. So you can count that as before the 28th of June, and he was definitely called Torben Hansen and not Thomas Hansen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It doesn't appear, in any event, Mr. Tapuskovic, that the witness can -- can help you, even if there is a second Hansen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Yes, all right. I acknowledge that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But at least then let me ask if he ever heard that representatives of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, either by sniper or shells, fired on their own people inside Sarajevo. Did he hear that from anyone during the five or six months that he was there, or not?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us move to the statement that you provided. First of all, that is correct was on the 25th of April, 1996 and then on the 5th and 14th of November here. That is document DD00-0584.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let us look at the first page, first, just to see if you can confirm that is indeed your statement. It's your statement, right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's my statement, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And we need to pay attention to the time, so we will move immediately to the third page of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: "It's not disputed that I arrived at the position on the 4th or the 5th of May." Here it says the 5th of May, but yesterday you said the 4th of May. But, anyway, it doesn't change things. You were at the post on the 5th of May, or the 4th. Yesterday, you said the 5th. It doesn't change the situation. Just confirm that for me, please.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I arrived on the 4th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, you said that already on the first day you were in danger in a way that you were missed -- that a sniper missed you by a mere 30 centimetres; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So in view of the positions where the two sides were, are you able to tell at all which side actually fired at you?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personal am not capable of telling you that, because it was my first hour or second hour in Sarajevo, and I was completely surprised by being shot at by somebody. So I didn't care who did do it. I don't recall that either. I couldn't establish that. So I fully trusted my -- my team commander, Captain Hansen, who was there for nearly six months, when he came up with the conclusion that this was a Serb sniper rifle, and I left it at that. I was lucky that I escaped.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let's not waste time on this. How was he able to say that it was a Serb sniper, since they were all up there on the hills separated by a few metres?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. He mentioned that, and I don't recall the discussion or the exchange of information we had on that moment. Again, I said I was happy to be -- to escape, and we went on with the business.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let's move to the statement, Mr. Konings. On page 3, and there -- it begins with the words "when I arrived" -- "on my arrival in Sarajevo." Do you see that paragraph on page 3?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you say here: "On my arrival in Sarajevo, the situation was very tense. It was shortly after the end of the cease-fire on the 1st of May, 1995." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Two paragraphs lower: "The situation deteriorated at the end of May and in June because of attacks by the Bosnian army."

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I read that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And that's how it was, right?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then it goes on to say: "On the 16th or the 17th of May, and then another time in June" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, again, in fairness to the context, it said, "The situation got worse, end of May and June, due to Bosnian army attacks on 16th and 17th May and another time in June and retaliation fire by the VRS."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please, reprisal is not mentioned here, but it says - I don't know if it is translated correctly - "against attacks by the army of Republika Srpska and counter-attack of the army of Republika Srpska." So first they were attacked in May and June, and then there was a counter-attack. That's what it says here. I don't know if it says "retaliation" or "counter-attack" in the English version. Perhaps the interpreters can help.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you have an English version in front of you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It says "retaliation."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, is it always retaliation when somebody responds to an attack, or is it one defending oneself from attack. There were attacks, and then it says "retaliation" from your side. Is it always retaliation if somebody is defending themselves?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now we are fighting about words, either defending or retaliation. In my statement then, apparently, I have used the word "retaliation." But you must be -- bear with me, I cannot remember every single word that I used, let's say, about 11 years ago. I know the whole scenery very well, what happened. And I can recall on the 16th and 17th of May, the Bosnian army started attacks to open ways out of Sarajevo. That is what they intended to do, what we learned later on. We couldn't conclude that on that day that there was heavy fighting going on. When an attack is going on, the guy you are attacking is retaliating. You can call it defending, whatever you like. The end result is that the two armies were shooting at each other in a massive way. The Bosnian army started this specific attacks on the 16th and 17th of May, and the Serb army responded to that in the same heavy way as the attacker did. The attacks failed, and the situation around Sarajevo only got more tense, and ended with the hostage taking of the Serb sides of the UNMOs and other people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. We have the explanation now of what was meant by "retaliation."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, at the beginning, you explained that you received the essential training necessary to examine impact craters and that several times you did go to investigate these craters. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever examine any craters on the Serb side, and do you know if they were any victims on the Serb side from attacks that took place in May and June, 1995?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I myself did no crater analysis on the Serb side because we were -- I was posted on the Bosnian army side. The UNMO organisation was such that there were also UNMOs posted at the Serb side of the confrontation line. There were several UNMO teams in the Sarajevo sector operational during May and June and also the period before, but I can only, of course, tell about the period when I arrived there. Two of my -- two of my Dutch colleagues coming in on the 4th of May, on the same date and same plane, went to the Serb side, and I still am in contact with them today. And I know that they did various crater analysis at the other side, and all there results were, as well as our results, sent to the UNMO HQ in Sarajevo and from there to Zagreb. I have no inside in these reports at that period, but we had numerous contacts with each other on the on the radio, and that situation stopped in June or at the end of May - I cannot recall that previously - when on the Serb side all the UNMOs were taken hostages, including my Dutch colleagues, and were taken out of order. So after, I think it was the end of May or the beginning of June, there were no UNMOs operational anymore at the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the same paragraph, you go on to say in the course of July and August, they were still firing but not that much until the Markale shelling. After this incident and the NATO air-strikes, the situation calmed down in Sarajevo. Is that how it was?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's exactly how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It was tense for four months because all of this and then after the NATO air-strikes the situation calmed down. NATO mostly targeted the Serb positions. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I -- what I know from the perspective that I had, and that is a very limited one being restricted to a team base. Because after the -- when the NATO air-strikes began, all UNMOs were restricted to their team bases so we were not allowed to move around anymore. And from my team base, I could see that NATO planes were attacking targets and the targets were outside of the confrontation lines, so in Serb territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Then we're going back to the events of the 28th. This is the next paragraph: "The next morning I drove to the UNMO HQ in the morning; after that I drove back, and when I arrived in my sector I heard on the radio that there had been an incident in the city." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You say: "The exact location of the incident was not known to me. I didn't know it, but there were casualties."

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was what was stated at that moment Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You knew that right away?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were in radio contact for a -- for example, also with OP1, and with my team base, and so the word had already been on the radio net that -- and by telephone, that there was an incident in the city with casualties and that was the only thing that we had heard so far. And being the team leader, I had ordered, especially my team base, that when any incident occurred - and they heard that by telephone - I would like to be informed by radio, so that's what they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, but look further on. What it says here is that you arrived home "and five minutes later I got a telephone from the Bosnian police who informed me about what had happened, and they asked us to come to the town." Therefore, you first received a telephone call from the Bosnian police. Is that true? Why did they call you specifically?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a normal procedure that the Bosnian police phoned one of the UNMO teams. And in this case the incident had happened in the AOR of my team, so they informed us that this had happened and asked us to come over to the -- to the site of the explosion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So you went there, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Yes, I went there, but you should read the following sentence to keep the picture complete. "I first contacted the HQ who agreed on our assistance in the investigation." Also that was standard operating procedure. Before we did business with anyone in the city, especially with the Bosnian police, we had to have permission from our HQ in the PTT building.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That is precisely what I wanted to ask you about. The first contact, your superiors, expecting your superiors to pass on the orders, or was it standard procedure for to you receive a call from the police and then you would contact your superiors. Was that the standard procedure?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between us and the Bosnian police there was no official standard procedure. The only standard procedure I can refer to was the with the commander at the HQ, but normally the Bosnian police phoned us, and in most cases they also phoned the HQ. Secondly, that was the standard procedure that no matter what happened we always, the team, always contacted the UNMO HQ in order to clarify what was said by the Bosnian police, who had called, what had happened, what had reported, and then we got either yes or no permission from the HQ to go on site and to do the investigation. There have been examples that the UNMO HQ refused us permission to go somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Further down on this page, you said that you found the tail of the mortar 50 metres away from the place of impact. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We found the tail of the mortar some metres -- yes. When I said the 50 metres, that must have been the 50 metres, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In the next paragraph, it reads as follows: "On the basis of this sign on the pavement, it was clearly the sign of a mortar explosion. On the basis of these signs, we determined the direction of fire. Our results were the same as the results of the Bosnian police and the results of French specialists on site." I know that it coincided with the results of the French specialists, but it did not coincide at all with the Bosnian findings. And you persisted in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Could we please have the reference on the screen so everybody, especially the witness, can follow. What part are we now talking about? Which page are we --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're still on page 3. I'm looking at the English version now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Will you just scroll down, I think, then we'll see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here you see 50 metres and immediately the paragraph after that. Towards the bottom of the page first it says where the tail was found and the next passage reads as follows: "On the basis of these signs we determined the direction of fire. Our results were the same as the results of the Bosnian police and it's results of French specialist." You said that the report addressed to Mr. Annan and your report coincided in full but that you did the want to accept the Bosnian police report which they tried to impose upon you that is correct the round came from the Serbian side. How do you account for that.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are now comparing pears and apples together so I have to clarify that once more. What we have -- what we compared on the scene on the site itself were the -- independently taken bearings the. We talk a bearing with our compass of 170 so we compare with the French specialist on side, first of all the engineers they came to 160 and we compare that with the results of the Bosnian police team. Also that we did always. We just compared it we not changed our measures because our measures we kept. Secondly, the bearing is something different than the discussion I had later on in the investigation team on the place of the origin of fire so the bearing was no secret. The bearing everybody could read on his own compass. What the Bosnian Committee of the Ministry of the Interior wanted me to say was that the fire came from Serb origin. And I reef fused that because I did not have -- I have not have the evidence to say that so there were two different things we are talking about. The bearing which is very clear, which you with measure on the spot, and the origin of fire which I could not say anything about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: On page 4 you say that you visited the scene where the other shells had landed. Let us find this particular paragraph. Also mention of the bearing. And you said that you visited the scene of the other four shell impacts and that there were casualties there as well. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, have I visited that other scene as well and did the investigation together with the same two colleagues as -- as on the other scene, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let us for a moment leave this document aside, and let us look at the document produced on the 6th of October, 2003, as a result of your meeting with Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's document DD00-0608.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me refer you to the passage where there's mention of the tail-fin of the shell. I think it's page 2 or 3 of the B/C/S version, or I should say the English version. So page 3, paragraph 4 in the English version. There's reference to the tail-fin of the shell. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I saw it, but now it's gone. But I saw it. Now I see it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At the top you said: "Immediately Konings recalls observing the tail-fin which was laying on the ground only 5 to 10 metres from the impact." First you said 50 metres and now in this interview with the Prosecutors you said 5 to 10 metres from the impact. Which of the two is correct?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can make an easy shot and make an average but that's not the -- not the idea to do. To be honest, it was at a certain distance from the place of impact and I cannot recall an exact distance, so I -- I cannot gives the right answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The next paragraph says -- it talks about the investigation of the other four rounds, and you said that there were casualties there. "According to Konings, investigation of the other four rounds took place more than four hours after they investigated Markale. The other four rounds were reported to have only caused damage to buildings and no deaths, so the killing round was focussed upon immediately." How do you explain that? You said that there had been casualties where these four rounds had fallen and that there were casualties. However, now you say that there were no casualties.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the first statement when I -- in 1996, which was the closest to my return, that was less than a year afterwards, that was correct. So there were some casualties, but there were not many only wounded people. But, again, then I start to go in the area of guessing and that's not right. So I would prefer, then, to stick to my first statement, which is in 1996, which is the closest to my appearance in Sarajevo, which said that there were certain victims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, we'll take the break now. I have to say that I have been corrected by the court deputy as to your time. When I said that you would have used 2 hours and 15 minutes by this break, in fact, according to the court deputy, you would have used 1 hour and 57 minutes. So much for my time-keeping. We'll resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. After the break, in order to gain time, I'm going to ask a few questions about these statements. So can we please have document DD00-0584, that's the statement dated the 26th of -- 22nd of April, be tendered as a Defence exhibit, please. I don't know if you heard me, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D119, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Also document DD00-0608, that's a statement dated the 6th of October, 2003, I would also like to tender it as a Defence exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D120, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, here I have a document, a report of the 3rd of September, 2003. That's a note of a telephone conversation between Colonel Konings and Mark Ierace, Jonathan Harris and Chester Stamp. That's DD00-0612. And I would like to ask the witness a few questions about it. The witness has, of course, the English version of this note, of this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Konings, did you have this telephone conversation on the 3rd of September, 2003 with members of the Prosecution whose names I have given you?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that I had a telephone conversation in 2003 with representatives of the ICTY. I cannot recall exactly whether it was the 3rd or the 4th or the 5th of September. But I definitely had this telephone call.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And as it says here, the subject of this conversation was the shelling of the Markale market of the 28th of August. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In this telephone conversation, in paragraph 3, you said the following to the interviewers: "I never met Powers or any other American while I was in Sarajevo, although about a year later I heard mention of an American investigation." Is that what you learned?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct, what I stated here. So about a year after I came back, there were some -- I heard some telling, and I think that was in the earlier investigation done by Belgium that there was also an American report on the incident. But I didn't know about it and I still don't know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But that's something that you learned, i.e., that a year later they investigated the Markale incident. Is it fair to say that?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard, again, one year later that apparently the Americans did -- some Americans or one American did an investigation on the Markale incident. That's all I can state.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Two paragraphs down it reads as follows. You said: "I sent my findings up the command chain. I knew from the media it had been decided that the Serbs did it." Is it true that only from the media did you find out that the incident in Markale had been caused by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But in relation to the questioning on 2000 and 2003, it has to be seen in relation with the former sentence: "I sent my findings up the command chain." So somewhere later, not on the same day as I told you before, since we had no possibility to watch TV or listen to the radio, a few days later, I think, I heard through the UNMO HQ that all the world was talking about this incident and accusing the Serbs of having done that. So that's up to the media, what they conclude, and not to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could it be that the media were more important and that their findings override the findings of expert bodies? What did you yourself think about this information?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only can say what I said many times before, that I saw what I saw. I wrote that down in a report; you have seen them. You have seen my ideas about that, that in combination with the fact that the OP1 had not heard or seen any outgoing round from Bosnian or Serb territory close to the vicinity of the OP, that my conclusion was that it must have come from Serb territory. But that's not inflicted by any media, so whatever the media say or whatever the media have for meaning on this, it doesn't matter to me in this case. The same is that I -- and I stated that here as well, is General Smith -- whatever General Smith decided, he was the highest ranking commander in UNPROFOR, but I did not know that at that time, I had no insight into his reports. I saw that -- all those things I saw later when I was contacted by the ICTY when they showed me that kind of letters or that kind of information. But on the spot, in the field, I never have seen this kind of relation -- this kind of reports from our commanders. The only thing I saw was my own report, my own handwritten report, and the summary our UNMO HQ in Sarajevo made the same evening and the evening afterwards. Those were the reports I have seen. And also what the media have said, I have had no contact with the media whatsoever. That was forbidden. We were not allowed to have any contact at all with any of the media. So that's what I can state to this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In the next sentence you said the following in this telephone conversation: "The conclusion that this was done by the Serbs was reached by General Smith." On what basis did you say that? Can you tell me that?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have that sentence on my screen, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It's in the same paragraph, paragraph 3 in the English version. No, no, no. One, two -- the fifth paragraph.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the fifth paragraph I have in front of me, there is no mentioning of General Smith whatsoever. My fifth paragraph says: "The Bosnians asked me to agree that the Serbs did it. As an UNMO, our job was to be impartial. I wrote down the facts of the explosion. Eventually I came to the conclusion that the Serbs did it." That is what the fifth lines says in mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The only reference is to General Smith is in the one, two three, fourth paragraph. "I knew from the media that it had been decided that Serbs did it. I'm not aware that the General Smith decided finally that it was the Serbs." Is that what you're referring to, Mr. Tapuskovic? Let's move on, because I'm not sure this is taking us anywhere, quite frankly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But Mr. Konings read the last paragraph, saying that he himself had reached the conclusion that this was done by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was it according to the media report or did you have any new facts? If you changed your mind later, why did you change it? Was it based on some additional facts subsequently found out?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was -- there were no change of opinion and there were no extra facts and I was definitely not influenced by the media. As I already stated in the first two reports, that the possibility that Serbs had done it were quite likely, although it was not -- there was no hard evidence of that. And the words I used here in my declaration to the ICTY is: "Eventually I came to the conclusion that the Serbs did it." There's no change of the facts. No other facts came in. I came to this conclusion based upon the facts as already -- as we have been discussing here before. So I don't need to add something to that. There was no extra evidence available when I said this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Konings, I have to ask you directly: If there were no new facts, then pressure was exerted on you from some side in order to justify the NATO action so -- that is, for you to change your opinion later. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. There is no change of opinion. The witness exactly explained the way he reached his conclusions. I think he said on that first document, his patrol report, that it was likely or highly likely that the Serbs did it. He referred to additional evidence he got from OP1. It's all consistent. There is no change of opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He does say: "Eventually I came to the conclusion that the Serbs did it," so there's the suggestion there of gradation, of movement, in opinion. I think there it's a fair question, because if there are no new facts, then it must be that you gave a different interpretation to the facts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you may call it that way, Your Honour; that after the years went over and I got this -- this question around again with the ICTY that you think it over and that I was more firm in my ultimate conclusion than I could do in -- in the time that I was in Sarajevo, that I came to this conclusion that the Serbs did it. And to be frankly, and I was not allowed to say that or to write it down, I think I had the same idea in the back of my mind already when I was in Sarajevo, on the spot when I saw what happened. But that's my personal opinion and that is not of interest for this Court, I think. But later on, the more I thought over the facts, and there were no extra facts and there was no pressure from any NATO body or from SFOR or IFOR or whatever organisation has been in the former Yugoslavia, that I came to this conclusion. It's purely my own thoughts about what I saw and what I wrote on a piece of paper that day, on a patrol report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm very satisfied with that answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to draw your attention to the third page, paragraph 9 in the English version of this conversation, page 3, paragraph 9, where a radar system is discussed. This is the Cymbelline system. Are you familiar that or aware that at the time of the event there was a British and Dutch very modern radar system to monitor outgoing and incoming fire?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know precisely that there was a Cymbelline radar system, which is the British radar system, that was in my AOR, as I stated that. I visited them sometimes. I had nothing to say on them. They were in the UNPROFOR chain of command. We didn't exchange information with them, so I had no idea what information they had. Of course, I knew, as an artillery man, what they were doing because I'm familiar with that kind of systems, and I knew that somewhere on Mount Igman NATO troops, or at least French, English and Dutch troops, were located and that there was also a Dutch radar operating. But that's all I know. I had no contacts with these people, because it was impossible to get on Mount Igman because we had no radio contact with them. Again, they were in a totally other chain of command than we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But in the report, the report of the 29th, you wrote that you had information that no one saw or heard a rocket from those places or a mortar projectile, either incoming or outgoing, and you stated that in your report and you did not change your original report in any way. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's absolutely correct. And when I say that no one heard or saw, then I refer to my own UNMO team. Everything I say and do has nothing to do with all other military organisations part -- being available in Sarajevo or outside Sarajevo. My only responsibility at that time was my UNMO team, the task we had to follow the commander's intent of my direct commander, which was senior military observer, and, if possible, to pay -- to take into account what other people reported to us, other UNPROFOR people. But we had to concentrate on our own work and our own team, so when I say no one heard or saw an outgoing round, I only talk about my own UNMOs and about nobody else, because I did not have any information on radar systems. I hardly knew who was on Mount Igman. I hardly knew that there were NATO troops on Mount Igman because we were deprived from any information whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there is a paragraph. I did not find a translation of that paragraph from this telephone conversation which states -- and that is actually on the basis of what I read earlier. It's on the third page. It should be on the last page, and it begins as follows: "OP ..." Your Honours, I said that I did not find that in the English version. I do have it in the Serbian version. This is on page 3. It's not there in the translation. It's not there in the English version and I'm going to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just to make sure that -- the original is certainly the English because that's the language the telephone interview was conducted, so that would sound very strange, that there is something in the translation which is not in the English original.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot explain it, but I'm going to read it. I don't speak English at all. I didn't consult my -- but I did look for it and I looked -- I didn't draft this. It has its number, 03039113. So I would like to read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's hear what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "OP1, observation posts, recall hearing the strikes but not outgoing shells. I am sure that they would have heard it had it come from the B and H army. That morning it was quiet and bright and they would have heard the firing had it come. I spent time at the observation post. Had the firing come immediately from the other side of the mountain, we would have heard it." And he said that even had the firing come from the other side of the mountain, you would have heard it. It's not there in the translation. I cannot explain it. Actually, it's not there in the English version, but if it is like that, it must have been omitted. I have no other explanation. I kept looking but perhaps I just missed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm trying to find it. Have you found it, Mr. Waespi?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Maybe Mr. Sachdeva can find it. Yes. It might be what we see on the screen right now. In the English version, it starts with "OP1. I recall that they heard the impacts ..." and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, we have seen it. What's the question you wish to put about that now? We have to move quickly now, Mr. Tapuskovic. You have gone some minutes now beyond the Prosecutor's time. What's the question that you have to put?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if it's true, what is written here, that had the firing come from the other side of the mountain it would have been heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have to be very careful with paraphrasing. If it can be put to the witness, the part what he said in his phone interview, OP1. It can be read to him, and he can confirm it yes or no. But this -- we can read the sentence. I think it's last two lines of that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. I will read it. It says, "That morning it was clear and quiet, and they must have heard it if they had been fired from within the confrontation lines." What is your response to that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I still stand with that declaration, and even more importantly is the next sentence. Even if it was fired "just from the other side of the mountain," you would have heard it, since I have done my duty there as well, which means -- and in that telephone conversation, I was not up to make conclusion, but that means that my conclusion was that the round came from further in Serb territory; so from a bigger distance, I would say at least three or four kilometres. That was my conclusion reading, having said that, et cetera, et cetera. So I have nothing more to add to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But it is being asserted here the whole time that it had it come from the Serb side, it wasn't heard because it was fired from the other side of the mountain. And here there's mentioned specifically that it would have been heard even had it come from the other side of the mountain. It's a very important issue, and this is what I am insisting upon as Defence counsel. Perhaps you didn't hear it, but others in other places would have heard it. Had it come from the other side of the mountain, it could not have happened -- or without it being unnoticed.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we tend to forget the word "just from the other side of the mountain," which means that the observers on OP1 didn't hear anything, not from close, not from the Bosnian army territory, not from the confrontation line, which you cannot overhearing being on OP1, that is absolutely true, and not just from the back of the mountains, which you can also -- which you could you hear. It just means they didn't hear anything, which is for me the conclusion that the round came from the southern direction further away than they could hear, which means that between the impact of the round and the point of origin of fire must have been at least a distance of about three, three and a half kilometres, which placed the origin of fire well into Serb territory. I cannot be more specific. I cannot be more clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Actually, Mr. Konings, you have just said something completely opposite from what it is said here. You said you did not hear it from your own position, but you said that had the shell been fired from the other side of the mountain, it would have been heard. You didn't hear it, but how do you explain that somebody else could have heard it?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't say I didn't hear it, because I didn't hear it. I was not even close to the vicinity. So my people there, the two people that we were talking about for already two days, Major Paul Conway and Major Thom Knustad, they were on OP1. They didn't hear any outgoing round. That is the first fact. The fact that they didn't hear any outgoing round makes it impossible that a round -- that the killing round was fired from Bosnian army territory because they would have heard it, and they would have seen it. It makes it also very -- very unlogic that it was fired from the confrontation line, because they would have heard it. It makes it also not very logic that it was fired from just behind the mountain ridge, because they would have heard it. The fact that they did not hear it means the only thing I can say about that is that it was fired from the southern direction at a distance from the point of impact of more than three or three and a half kilometre, which muffles the sound so that they could not hear it. So it placed the point of origin of the round well into Serb territory. And that's the most clear way I can explain what I have said here in this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Konings, at the place where the crater was, did you find the shell casing left after the impact of the shell? Did you find a groove or something, the scratch left by the shell? Did you find anything like that at that location?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You don't -- after an explosion, you don't find a shell casing, at least the word I understand casing. The shell explodes and you only find shrapnels. It is very simple. And if you are lucky, you find a piece of the fuse; and if you -- and in all occasions with this type of mortar projectile, you find the tail. So you don't find the casing, you find thousands of parts of the casing if you are looking for them. So shrapnels were found on the location -- on various locations around the impact.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When a shell hits, does it leave a trail? Does it leave a channel? Did you find that, the channel that the shell made before impact?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you refer to the fuse furrow, which is the impact area where the fuse hits the ground. First of all, we saw a very clear crater with a very small impact, deeper impact which was the place, to our opinion, where the fuse hit the ground. So we took that as the central part of the crater; and since the crater was very clear - we all saw it on the picture behind me yesterday - we could easily take the bearing from which direction the round came.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't have time to go back to statements that have already been tendered. You claim that you did it not find a fuse furrow on the site. The third time I'm asking you: Did you find at the location a fuse furrow left by the shell fuse?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, what I already stated is that we found the spot where we -- that we designated as being the point of impact of the -- the projectile. That was on that moment enough for to us establish, and the French engineers did exactly the same, to take it as the point of impact and not to bother about whether it this was a deeper fuse furrow, yes or no. It was clearly the deepest point in -- in the whole area precisely fitted with the pattern of the -- the crater. So we have taken that as the point of impact, and you can call that the fuse furrow, but we did not call it that way in our report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please, I'm going to show you from this telephone conversation, last paragraph from page 2. That would be the entire paragraph. Can you please find page 2, the last paragraph, and you say here: "The visual crater analysis on killing round impact, clear impact. It was fresh, and we found the tail close by. We did a compass bearing to determine the bearing. We did not use a stick into the furrow because there was none on the concrete surface of the road. We improvised. It had a distinct crater, and without a stick you are able to measure the bearing. We did not use the stick method. There was a shallow fuse furrow. I cannot recall why we did not use the stick." Thus, you did say that the fuse did make a shallow furrow. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stated that on -- in September 2003. That is absolutely correct. And the thing I said before, that you have a small impact crater inside the whole pattern, I said you can call it the fuse furrow. On the moment we were there, we just looked for the deepest point inside the crater, which is -- which is apparently the fuse furrow, but we didn't call it that way in our report. And the name furrow, fuse furrow, came later on up in the reports, as it is the technical name nor that deeper point in the crater.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Witness, can I just ask you: Where would you expect, under normal circumstances, to find the tail-fin of a 120-millimetre mortar grenade, if it had impacted on a tarmac or on the road like it did here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say anything about a specific bearing or distance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: No, no. Would you expect to find the tail-fin inside the crater or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, definitely not inside the crater, somewhere in the broader area; and that depends partly on the ground where it explodes, on the angle of impact of the projectile, whether it is in exploding in the open or in a closed area. So there are many factors, but I haven't seen on any occasion that it was found inside the smaller part of the crater.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Konings, then go on to say that you cannot explain why you did use the stick, even though you did fine a furrow; and then you continue: "There were angry people and body parts all around, maybe that is why we did not use the stick." Had you used the stick, perhaps you would have obtained more reliable date. Why did you not use the stick when it was your duty to ignore what was happening around you and to do your job properly? Why didn't you use the stick when you had a furrow?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can refer to what I said. I cannot recall why we did not use a stick. One argument, which I can place as an extra, is that the fuse furrow was very shallow. It was in concrete or in tarmac. It's not very ease to put a stick in that, so it doesn't work since you don't have equipment for that as well. But since the fuse furrow was clear, since the pattern was very clear, you could divide it in two and a halves, left and right, so could you take the middle line of the pattern. It was enough for us on that moment, seeing the tense situation, that we did our work in that way and that we decided to do it without the stick method, because the stick method didn't work in tarmac or asphalt. And I'm still convinced about the fact that the bearing we took was accurate enough for providing a report that I have been written. If I had used the stick method, if it was possible at all - I doubt that in tarmac - we would not have come to a total different solution. Maybe it would have been a variation of, let's say, between zero and five degrees, but it would still point in the southern direction where the projectile came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this document DD00-0612 be tendered into evidence as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D121, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And you should be bringing this to an end now, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I use at least these ten or 12 minutes that are be left. Your Honours, I really need to do this. I still have this statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you going to re-examine, Mr. Waespi?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Not until now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, we'll give you another five until 7.00 -- eight minutes until five to 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to show the witness the statement of the 31st of May 2006. This is DD00-0621, statement of the 31st of May of Mr. Konings. You've already seen this, and you've confirmed that. But here it is now, time is passing. DD00-0621. This is your statement. You've already --

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. That's my statement, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can with he go right to paragraph 13, so I can just briefly ask you. This is the Markale investigation. This is approximately page 4, but it's paragraph 13. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 13, in the middle, I don't want to read everything because I don't have time: "At Markale on the 28th of August 1995, I did not see a fuse funnel." How do you explain now that you said that you did not see a fuse funnel?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I stated is that we saw a very shallow impact area, which you can hardly call a fuse furrow. We didn't find any remainings of the fuse as well. So the only thing we saw is a very shallow, let's say, area where the -- where the projectile hit -- hit the ground. And there is nothing more to add to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I may have used another one half-hours in -- on this topic; however, I would just request that this document DD00-0621 be entered as Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D122, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You would have spent another hour and a half on this topic, you said. That would have been an abuse, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that would only be appropriate time for me to do the proper examination; however, I respect every decision taken by the Chamber. I'm satisfied that this document has been admitted into evidence, and I'm going to use it in the course of these proceedings. Now, briefly, document DD00-1414, dated the 4th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned this information yesterday, and you said that people were on the pavement. First, look here. You said that people were on sidewalks. Pavements were hardly two metres wide. Here you said "pavements." You never mentioned sidewalks.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pavements and sidewalks to me belong to the street; and to make it all clear, people were all over the street, including the sidewalks. So if I said "sidewalks" during my investigation with Mr. Waespi on the 9th of March, I have to recollect. I have to -- to maybe to restate that and say the whole street, because people were in the middle of the street, on the pavement, including the sidewalks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: My question is: How could they have been on --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: The counsel is using the B/C/S word "plocnik," which means pavement and sidewalk. It seems that he is referring to the road or the lanes where cars drive.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm referring to that as well, so what I mean to say is that there were people on the lanes where normally the cars are driving. So we had trouble to pass by because it was very busy, and people were also on the sidewalks, the two metres on the side of the street, where people were sitting, walking. In fact, the basic thing is there were literally hundreds of people crowded all over the street, including on every sidewalk, sidestep, or how you call it in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, you said an hour or two, but here you said a few hours before the incident you passed there in your car. You didn't walk?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never have said that I walked there, at least that I can recall it. I drove in my car, passing along the Markale place, and that was indeed a few hours before. So I was there around 9.00, 9.30, somewhere around that time. That is what I know for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if you passed a few hours earlier that would make it 8.00 a.m. You said that you didn't see the crater at that time, and the crater wasn't there at the time because the explosion occurred three hours later.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not there at 8.00. As I said just a minute ago, I was there around 9.00 or 9.30; and at that moment, it was very crowded on the streets. There were hundreds of people on the street, completely covering the whole street. I was driving in my car, and again, it was 9.30 and the crater was not there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, you have asked the last question. Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it, and you may now leave. But we will adjourn and resume tomorrow at 2.15.
